message.content:
**Gini coefficient – United States**

| Source | Year reported | Value | Notes |
|--------|---------------|-------|-------|
| **World Bank – World Development Indicators (WDI)** | 2021 (latest estimate) | **≈ 41.5** | This figure refers to *pre‑tax* income distribution measured at the household level. It’s based on national accounts and surveys compiled by the U.S. Census Bureau and other agencies. |
| **OECD Income Distribution Database** | 2019 (most recent full survey cycle) | ≈ 40.5 | Uses post‑tax & transfer incomes; slightly lower than the World Bank value because taxes and transfers reduce inequality. |

### Quick takeaways

- The U.S. sits roughly mid‑range among high‑income countries—higher than many European peers (~35–38), but below some emerging economies (>45).
- The Gini has been relatively stable over the past decade, hovering around 41–42 when measured before taxes/transfers.
- After accounting for government redistribution, the effective Gini drops to the low 30s.

#### Where you can verify / update this yourself

- **World Bank DataBank:** Search “GINI” under the indicator list → choose “United States” and set the time period.  
- **OECD iLibrary:** Navigate to “Income Inequality” > “Data” tab → select “USA” and pick the most recent year.  

If you’re looking for even newer estimates (e.g., 2023), keep an eye on releases from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey (CPS) or the American Community Survey (ACS); they publish quarterly updates that feed into both World Bank and OECD calculations.

Or use OECD: 39.7 (2009) but older. So best to say approx 41.5 as per World Bank 2021. Also note difference between pre-tax vs after tax etc. Provide citation.
